entry.title: Chaos and bifurcations in continuous language-model feedback
entry.summary: Feeding a pretrained language model the expected embedding of its own next-token distribution turns it into a discrete-time dynamical system with continuous states. Across Qwen2.5, OLMo-2 and Llama-3 models from 0.5B to 72B parameters, temperature and activation steering move this loop between repeating text and chaos, with positive finite-time Lyapunov exponents. The loop's derivative factorizes into the inverse temperature, the covariance of token embeddings under the next-token distribution (a cross-covariance for untied embeddings) and the network's Jacobian. In one model studied in detail, along recorded orbits, the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout, where next tokens compete. The periodic windows show the quantitative signatures of low-dimensional maps, from saddle-node scaling and Feigenbaum's constant to shrimp-shaped domains; passage times predicted in advance from the model's derivatives came within one return-map iterate of the measured passage times in 42 of 48 cases over two prospective stages (24 and 18 of 24), and interval arithmetic proves attracting periodic orbits of the full transformer map. Numerical reproducibility depends on the dynamical regime: changing only the batch layout changed the text of 173 of 192 chaotic float64 loops in the smallest model, compared with only 7 of 192 periodic ones. These results show that bifurcation theory can make quantitative predictions about continuous language-model feedback, with rigorous guarantees for selected periodic orbits of the full transformer.

entry.title: Chaos and scrambling in anisotropic Dicke and Rabi models
entry.summary: Identifying the quantum signatures of classical chaos remains a central question in quantum physics, and quantum scrambling provides a new perspective on this correspondence. We study two distinct limits of the same model to examine how the correspondence between chaos and scrambling changes across different regimes. The thermodynamic-limit anisotropic Dicke model exhibits a close correspondence between chaos and scrambling, whereas this correspondence breaks down in the large-frequency-ratio limit of the anisotropic Rabi model (ARM). The contrasting chaotic behavior in the two limits originates from the different numbers of classical degrees of freedom, whereas their similar scrambling behavior stems from eigenstate delocalization. This implies that, in the large-frequency-ratio limit, eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to qualify the ARM as a classically chaotic model. This finding suggests that identifying chaos in quantum systems requires jointly considering the classical degrees of freedom and eigenstate delocalization.

entry.title: Scrambling Separates Superradiance from Quantum Chaos
entry.summary: Early studies on the Dicke model linked superradiance to quantum chaos, whereas later anisotropic Dicke and Rabi studies reached apparently conflicting conclusions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing global chaos from local instability. Along the isotropic Dicke path, a sweep at fixed low excitation energy crosses both the superradiant boundary and a nearby chaotic window, explaining the reported correlation. However, the anisotropic Dicke model can be chaotic in the normal phase and regular in the superradiant phase, making superradiance neither necessary nor sufficient for global chaos. A fidelity out-of-time-order correlator (FOTOC), in contrast, probes the local stability of the stationary point selected by the initial wave packet. The superradiant transition destabilizes the origin, whereas a change in anisotropy can restore its stability and create displaced saddles. Wave packets centered at these saddles exhibit exponential FOTOC growth even on a classically regular Dicke energy shell with Poisson statistics. This local sensitivity also enables quantitative spectroscopy: combined with the topology of stationary points and local density of states relations, FOTOC dynamics reconstructs the absolute amplitudes of spectral singularities in both models without fitting the density of states.
entry.arxiv:comment: 15 pages (6-page main text and 9-page Supplemental Material), 9 figures, 4 tables

entry.title: Classical-to-Quantum Transition in Blackbody Radiation Thermodynamics: Planck's Law without Statistical Assumptions
entry.summary: Inspired by Fermi's model of radiation-matter interaction, we investigate the classical dynamics of a closed, finite-energy system, in which matter is coupled to an electromagnetic field. We find that energy is progressively transferred to increasingly high-frequency field modes, so that the effective temperature of both matter and radiation approaches zero in the long-time limit - in sharp contradiction with the finite-temperature equilibrium assumed by classical blackbody thermodynamics. Requiring consistency with the Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws identifies a characteristic time $t_L$, at which both laws are simultaneously satisfied. Strikingly, classical spectra obtained for different energies and cavity sizes collapse onto the universal Planck distribution at $t_L$. We conjecture that quantum dynamical localization arrests the classical energy cascade at $t_L$, and that the Planck distribution emerges as a dynamical consequence of this arrest - without invoking any a priori statistical assumption.

entry.title: Physics-Inspired Optimizers beyond the Edge of Stability: Period-Two Orbits and Delayed Instability
entry.summary: Gradient descent with momentum can be viewed as a particle moving with friction in the loss landscape. In deep learning the learning rate is usually large, so training is a discrete dynamical system: in many full-batch experiments the sharpness grows to the optimizer's stability limit, the edge of stability (EoS), and training continues there. Physics-inspired optimizers change this motion; Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam), for example, shrinks the step at high speed. We study kinetic maps, in which the step is the gradient of a kinetic energy of the momentum, and ask what they do beyond the EoS. (i) In a reduced model, a kinetic map creates a symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge, strictly linearly stable if and only if the map's elasticity (the log-log slope of step length versus momentum) lies between 0 and 1; on it, training sits at an effective edge of stability. VRAdam's damper fails above twice the critical learning rate, where its kinetic energy is not convex; the Legendre dual of VRAdam's own Lagrangian is convex and passes at every learning rate. (ii) Because the sharpness rises gradually, the loss of stability is delayed, as in Neishtadt's theory of slowly swept bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the dynamics match this theory without fitted parameters, including the memory of where the sweep started and its erasure by noise. (iii) With momentum, reaching the oscillation also requires elasticity at large momentum: maps that bound the step have competing period-four and chaotic attractors already at beta1 = 0.9, while the cubic-Legendre map reached the oscillation from every sampled start up to beta1 = 0.99. Experiments on an exact quadratic problem, a full-batch MLP and ResNet-32 support the theory; on ResNet-18, much of the apparent benefit of the maps is reproduced by matching the effective learning rate.

entry.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
entry.summary: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket (a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior) can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, reproduce, and die. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux increases the dependence. We argue that this is because flux is a statistical collider. Conditioning on the boundary's own concentration state screens about a fifth of the nonlinear dependence. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field of that thickness does screen the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would; this is not evidence of inference.

entry.title: Shearless and periodic attractors in the dissipative Labyrinthic map
entry.summary: The Labyrinthic map is a two-dimensional area-preserving map that features a robust transport barrier known as the shearless curve. In this study, we explore a dissipative version of this map,examining how dissipation affects the shearless curve and leads to the emergence of quasi-periodic or chaotic attractors, referred to as shearless attractors. We present a route to chaos of the shearless attractor known as the Curry-Yorke route. To investigate the multi-stability of the system, we employ basin entropy and boundary basin entropy analyses to characterize diverse scenarios. Additionally, we numerically investigate the dynamic periodic structures known as "shrimps" and "Arnold tongues" by varying the parameters of the system.
entry.arxiv:journal_ref: L. F. B. Souza, R. Egydio de Carvalho, R. L. Viana, I. L. Caldas; Shearless and periodic attractors in the dissipative Labyrinthic map. Chaos 1 December 2024; 34 (12): 123132

entry.title: Fate of Arnold tongues and canards in Mobius systems with noise
entry.summary: We consider a class of noisy dynamical systems on the two-dimensional torus whose phase evolution is governed by Mobius transformations. In the deterministic limit, these systems favor phase-locking that is described by the band-gap structure of an associated Schrodinger equation with a periodic potential. We use the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin method to characterize this structure in the slow-fast limit. Then we show that large-deviation theory describes fluctuations of the finite-time rotation number, whereas weak-noise escape actions determine the exponential scale of rare phase slips. These estimates provide quantitative criteria for metastable phase-locking and melting of Arnold tongues over a prescribed observation time. We derive sufficient conditions for stochastic trajectories to follow prescribed canard segments. With controlled entrance errors, exponential amplification of fluctuations along repelling branches leads to an exponentially small sufficient noise scale for canard persistence in the slow-forcing limit.

entry.title: Eclipse Observables for Navigation in Cislunar Space
entry.summary: Autonomous navigation independent of Earth-based tracking remains a challenge for spacecraft operating in cislunar space. This paper proposes onboard eclipse detection as an opportunistic measurement set to supplement the state estimation of cislunar trajectories. Penumbral and umbral entry and exit times detected from standard power telemetry are formulated as implicit zero-measurements on the boundaries of second-order shadow cones computed from planetary ephemerides. These observables are processed in an unscented Kalman filter. The event-time uncertainty that weights each measurement is derived from physical sources excluded in the spherical body model, including telemetry sampling, Earth's atmosphere, and topography/oblateness of the occulting body. The approach is demonstrated both in simulation for an $L_1$ halo orbit and with flight telemetry and orbit determination products from the CAPSTONE spacecraft during the January 2026 lunar eclipse, where umbral contacts timed directly from the power telemetry agree with the geometric contacts to within one sample interval. In both cases, hardware-free eclipse event timing shows utility in uncertainty reduction, especially as the initial solution quality is degraded.
entry.arxiv:comment: Submitted to the AIAA Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets on 10/16/2026

entry.title: From Flow-Box Invariants to Global Conservation Laws: Machine Learning-Assisted Detection of Singularities and Near-Integrability
entry.summary: Conservation laws reveal invariant structure in dynamical systems and constrain their evolution to lower-dimensional level sets. Locally, however, per the flow-box theorem, every $d$-dimensional system generically admits $d-1$ functionally independent conservation laws near a regular point even though, generically, only a few such laws persist globally. Data-driven methods typically learn conservation laws on a prescribed region of phase space from which training samples are drawn, leaving their behavior beyond that region unresolved. We formulate this local-to-global continuation problem and develop an {expanding-domain neural deflation} framework that tracks the number of independent conservation laws over nested domains. The method recovers the expected $d-1$ local invariants and detects their successive breakdown as the domain expands, relaxing to the expected global conservation law limit. It distinguishes the local invariants (associated with Frobenius integrability) from persistent global structure and shows that the domain scale over which additional laws survive reflects proximity to Liouville integrability. Pointwise losses can localize isolated obstructions, whereas in more complicated dynamics the breakdown of our loss functions is gradual and spatially diffuse. The framework thus provides a data-driven approach for studying the persistence and breakdown of (so-far-learned) conservation laws across phase space.

entry.title: Action-Quantized Scar Multiplets and Dissipative Cat States from Fractal Period-Locking in the Open Quantum Baker Map
entry.summary: We open the quantum baker map with a position window of width $w$ and center $q_c$. Classical pruning tiles the $(q_c,w)$ plane into diamonds where the $T$ leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At $w=1/2$ one periodic orbit survives for almost every $q_c$, and the multiplets are quantized without free parameters: their modulus $2^{-1/2}$ saturates the pressure bound and their phase is the orbit action. They form cycling multicomponent cat states, and the opening becomes one mid-circuit measurement, enabling spectroscopy with $\sim10^2$ shots on quantum processors.
entry.arxiv:comment: 6 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material (7 pages) included

entry.title: Synchronization over Resource-Causal Temporal Networks with Consumable Entanglement Links
entry.summary: When communication consumes shared entanglement, a physical link does not guarantee that an interaction is available. We study synchronization of classical continuous-time systems whose interactions consume randomly replenished resources stored on edges. Under isotropic tangent coupling and state independent scheduling, the linearized evolution separates exactly into intrinsic node growth and an ordered product of communication matrices. This yields temporal contraction conditions and local nonlinear synchronization. Resource conservation bounds the contraction achievable by every schedule with acyclic event services. On a fixed acyclic orientation with a unique source, serving each ready edge immediately is optimal: the non-source node with the least total incoming supply determines the rate. Balanced incoming supplies attain the bound. For linear coupling on these orientations, a further condition guarantees synchronization throughout a convex invariant domain. In the specified Lorenz domain, this sufficient contraction requirement is about three percent above a necessary requirement for uniform exponential synchronization. Kuramoto simulations illustrate the effect of service direction, while Lorenz simulations compare resource policies and test local growth predictions against finite-time dynamics.
entry.arxiv:comment: 12 pages, 5 figures; includes a 1-page numerical verification supplement

entry.title: SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE: High-performance finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov-exponent computations for CPUs and GPUs
entry.summary: Finite-time and finite-size Lyapunov exponents (FTLE and FSLE) characterise material stretching and transport barriers over prescribed time intervals and separation scales, but their evaluation from three-dimensional velocity sequences requires large computational costs. We introduce SCP-FTLE and SCP-FSLE, two modules of StreamCenter+ for CPU- and GPU-accelerated Lagrangian analysis. The modules support structured and native unstructured meshes, selectable integration and interpolation schemes, and graphical and command-line workflows. Rolling snapshot reuse, memory-bounded FTLE batching, device-resident trajectory state and active-set FSLE advancement reduce data movement and redundant computation, achieving the state-of-the-art (SOTA) computational performance among peer packages. For a billion-seed benchmark, strong-scaling efficiencies on 32 GPUs reach 86.3% for FTLE and 95.2% for FSLE. FTLE is verified with published steady and unsteady Arnold-Beltrami-Childress (ABC) flows and stationary concentrated vortex model (SCVM), while FSLE is verified in linear stretching and rotational shear flows. As examples, applications reveal the spanwise reorganisation of stretching layers in a shear-thinning lid-driven cavity, and resolve three-dimensional stretching structures associated with contrasting tracer dispersion around an urban building canopy at NUS campus. These results demonstrate a scalable workflow in large-scale Lagrangian diagnostics and analysis of flow data.

entry.title: Time-reversible timestepping in many-body planetary systems
entry.summary: Simulating chaotic planetary system evolution requires resolving small time-scales due to close encounters, scattering, collisions, and more. Simulations typically assign fixed timesteps to all particles, however, which is inefficient and wastes compute resources in a chaotically evolving system; moreover, it may under-resolve the simulation. Hybrid methods are a blunt tool for resolving small time-scales as they do not allow for fine-grained adaptation. Assigning individual timesteps, which vary in time, to planetary bodies usually violates desirable properties such as symplecticity and reversibility. In this work, we develop an "almost" exactly time-reversible direct $N$-body integrator, MTR, in which each pair of planets gets its own timestep, which itself can vary as the system evolves. In contrast to our previous work, we achieve this adaptation on the fly, independent of a global timestep. We provide a C version of the code and test it on several problems, demonstrating no energy error drift, as expected of a reversible method. At large particle numbers, up to $N = 975$, we compare against the state-of-the-art GPLUM code, which we can use in direct Hermite mode (for which it is not optimized) or tree mode (for which it is). MTR provides a speedup of up to two orders of magnitude compared to the Hermite mode, while agreeing with the distribution of orbits. In our default configuration, MTR's speed matches or improves on the tree mode's speed, by up to an order magnitude, despite the tree mode's faster and approximate force calculation.

entry.title: Ordinal-pattern transition networks as a symbolic substrate for reservoir computing
entry.summary: Reservoir computing has established itself as a computationally efficient alternative to fully trained recurrent neural networks using a fixed high-dimensional nonlinear substrate to map temporal input into a feature space for a simple readout. Here, we argue that reservoir computing can be realized entirely within a coarse-grained, symbolic state space, and that constrained random walks on ordinal-pattern transition networks provide a natural instance of this realization, replacing the reservoir's continuous state space with a discrete and directly data-derived one. We develop a formal correspondence between the two frameworks, show that the echo-state property has a natural discrete analog in the ergodicity and spectral gap of the walk's underlying Markov chain, and illustrate the correspondence with a minimal example and an empirical one-step-ahead prediction task evaluated across five paradigmatic model systems. These systems exhibit dynamics that correspond to strictly periodic, quasiperiodic, chaotic, or stochastic signals. We argue that this symbolic reservoir perspective allows a redefinition of the reservoir substrate itself, replacing the requirement of a continuous, randomly generated dynamical system with any sufficiently ergodic, data-derived symbolic process. This opens a route toward interpretable, data-adaptive reservoirs whose internal structure is inferred rather than randomly assigned, with implications for surrogate-data methods and reservoir design more broadly.

entry.title: A general feedback mechanism unifying stochasticity, long transients, and resilience
entry.summary: Stochasticity in complex systems is commonly treated either as external noise added to deterministic dynamics or as an effective stochastic description of deterministic chaos. A framework in which stochastic dynamics arise endogenously from deterministic chaos and subsequently feed back on the deterministic dynamics, thereby fundamentally reshaping system dynamics, remains rare. Here, we develop such a framework. Through the interaction between deterministic and stochastic dynamics, alternative stable states, critical transitions, adaptive capacity, stochasticity, and resilience become dynamically interconnected within a single model. Furthermore, the framework establishes a new mechanism of long transients, driven by two key factors: (i) time-scale separation and (ii) time-delay-induced cancellation. Stochasticity plays a dual stabilizing-destabilizing role in long transients: it promotes their persistence while also facilitating their eventual escape and collapse. This dual role allows resilience to be quantified dynamically through escape and stochastic recapture dynamics. Finally, we establish the generality of the mechanism mathematically and numerically across a broad class of one-dimensional nonlinear systems, suggesting that it reflects a general dynamical principle.

entry.title: Pantograph Difference Equations: Stability, Multistability, and Chaos
entry.summary: Pantograph equations are functional differential equations with proportional delay, typically involving terms of the form $x(at)$, where $0<a<1$. These equations have been studied for several decades and have applications in areas ranging from number theory to electrodynamics. In this work, we investigate pantograph difference equations as discrete dynamical maps of the form \[ x_{i+1}=F(x_{i})+G(x_{h(i)}), \qquad i\geq 0, \] where $h(i)\leq i$. In particular, we consider $h(i)=\lfloor ai \rfloor$ and $h(i)=\lfloor ai^α\rfloor$, with $0<a<1$ and $0<α<1$. We distinguish between homogeneous pantograph difference equations, for which $F(x)=0$, and inhomogeneous pantograph difference equations, for which $F(x)\ne 0$. We first analyze linear pantograph difference equations and establish sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability and for nonconvergence to zero. For proportional delays, analytical stability and instability regions are combined with multi-horizon parameter scans to construct regime diagrams in the $(λ,δ)$-plane. We then investigate pantograph versions of the logistic and tent maps. In the homogeneous case, the dynamics evolves through step-like plateaus whose lengths increase at least exponentially, leading to slow convergence and finite-time multistability within computationally accessible time scales. In the inhomogeneous case, numerical experiments show finite-time exponential separation of nearby trajectories, consistent with chaotic dynamics.

entry.title: Statistical Characterization of Erratic and Chaotic Processes through Their Extrema I. Thermodynamics
entry.summary: We propose a general statistical framework for characterizing erratic functions through the statistics of their extrema, with the aim of identifying statistical signatures associated with chaotic processes. It is based on analyzing the extrema points of erratic functions associated with these processes. One is instructed to determine the probability distribution functions ( PDF)s of the locations of the extrema points, the spacings between the locations, in particular the nearest neighbors, and the ratios between adjacent spacings. We then fit these PDFs with PDFs known to relate to chaotic behavior like of random matrix theory. The extrema considered establish a cloud of points in general in $D$ dimensions for erratic function of several variables. For certain systems one finds also extrema curves. We further determine the ``thermodynamic" description of the erratic functions by computing the Shannon or differential entropy and by equating the PDFs to the Gibbs one. With this map we determine the ``energy function" and for certain cases also the ``temperature". We analyze three benchmark spacing PDFs: the Bernoulli shift map, the Poisson and the Gaussian beta ensemble and several others. We want to emphasize that the map to thermodynamics can be applied to variety of chaotic processes including non-physics ones. We distinguish marginal spacing distributions from joint distributions of consecutive spacings. The latter probe correlations and statistical organization that are invisible in one-spacing PDFs and may provide stronger signatures for distinguishing structured chaotic-like behavior from uncorrelated irregularity.

entry.title: Dynamical phase transition for a logarithm observable in chaotic systems
entry.summary: We consider the full distribution $P_N(A)$ of the dynamical observable $A = - \sum_{i=1}^N \ln x_i$ where $x_1, \dots, x_N$ is a sequence generated by a chaotic map $f(x)$ via $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$. We study the particular cases where $f(x)$ is the doubling, tent or logistic map, and focus on the limit $N \gg 1$. Typical fluctuations of $A$ are Gaussian with mean $\left\langle A\right\rangle$ and variance which are both of order $\sim N$. We find that the left tail of the distribution ($A < \left\langle A\right\rangle$) scales as $P_{N}(A) \sim e^{-NI(A/N)}$, and calculate the rate function $I(a)$ which depends on the map $f(x)$. Interestingly, we find that the right tail of the distribution ($A > \left\langle A\right\rangle$) follows an anomalous scaling: $P_{N}(A) \sim e^{-N^{1/3} F((A-\left\langle A\right\rangle) / N^{2/3})}$. The large-deviation function $F(y)$ has a universal form for the three maps, differing only in the scaling constants. At a critical value $y=y_c$, it exhibits a corner singularity which has the character of a condensation transition. The transition separates between a subcritical phase $0< y<y_c$ in which the fluctuations are Gaussian and arise homogeneously from all of the $x_i$'s, and a supercritical phase $y>y_c$ in which a small fraction of the $x_i$'s give a macroscopic contribution to the fluctuation. Despite this anomalous behavior of the right tail, we find that the cumulants of the distribution $P_N(A)$ grow linearly with $N$ at large $N$, and calculate the associated coefficients.

entry.title: A Panoramic Network Overview of Shortcut Impact on Power Grids
entry.summary: Synchronization of coupled oscillators on complex networks underlies critical functions in natural and engineered systems, including power-grid operation. While synchronization stability on fixed network topologies has been studied extensively, less is known about how an added transmission link affects stability depending on where it is placed relative to generation and consumption. We address this question using simplified ring-network power-grid models in which producer and consumer nodes are spatially organized into clusters. Long-range transmission links, which we refer to as shortcuts, are added between non-adjacent nodes, and synchronization stability is quantified by basin stability in second-order coupled-oscillator dynamics. We compare shortcut placements across four scenarios varying network size, power allocation, power-injection heterogeneity, and producer--consumer arrangement. When producers and consumers form two spatially separated clusters, center-to-center shortcuts do not reduce the mean basin stability in the configurations examined and increase it by up to 75\% relative to the shortcut-less baseline. Peripheral shortcuts instead reduce mean basin stability by up to 28\% in some configurations despite the added connection, producing Braess-like degradation. In alternating multi-block networks, however, no single shortcut placement provides the same substantial enhancement, indicating that the center-to-center advantage does not directly generalize to more complex spatial arrangements. Representative time-domain simulations further show faster decay of frequency deviations for center-to-center than for peripheral shortcuts. These results demonstrate that the effect of added connectivity depends critically on where the new link is placed relative to the spatial organization of generation and consumption.

entry.title: Mathematics of Herding
entry.summary: A herd of animals often follows a leader who sets the direction of travel. The leader sometimes turns unexpectedly and the followers reshuffle. Yet the herd regroups itself and stays coherent. Our work aims to understand the herding behavior mathematically. We construct a minimal discrete-time nonequilibrium dynamical system with one-way coupling, and the minimal structure allows an exact analysis. Take the location of each follower in the frame of the leader. The recorded locations form a distribution. The limit of the distribution is the asymptotic spatial measure, whose geometric representation we study. The dynamics of the herd have an exact operator representation with two factors, the operator of a fixed leader-follower pair and the operator of the interaction rules, which reshuffle the pairs. We show that the influence of the leader passes through some follower more than once. As a result, two followers can have reciprocal influence, despite the one-way coupling.

entry.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
entry.summary: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

entry.title: Online training of Echo State Networks to predict chaotic dynamical systems
entry.summary: Echo State Networks (ESNs) are fundamentally important from the conceptual perspective of AI, because they provide simple and tractable frameworks for understanding temporal information processing, memory, and learning in dynamical systems. They are composed by an interconnected reservoir whose connectivity matrix remains constant over time and only the output weights are updated during the training period. In particular, ESNs employing online training allow the incremental adaptation of the output weights as data is received, making them particularly suitable for applications in which new input data becomes available over time (non-stationary environments). A key objective in the study of such learning structures is to determine which statistical properties of the reservoir enhance computational efficiency and maximize prediction performance. To this end, we investigate the effects of reservoir topology on learning performance, considering weight matrices generated from Erdos-Renyi random networks and Watts & Strogatz small-world networks. As test data we use the Lorenz and Rossler models in the chaotic regime and the FitzHugh-Nagumo model in the limit cycle regime. In the case of random Erdos-Renyi reservoirs, our simulations show that best performances are obtained for sparse reservoirs and especially when the link-density is near and immediately above the critical point of mean-field bond percolation. Watts & Strogatz reservoirs are shown to demonstrate best performance also for small values of link-density, compatible with the mean-field bond percolation when taking into account the specific nonlocal ring structure of the Watts & Strogatz reservoirs. These studies on the influence of the reservoir architecture and hyperparameters on enhancing the accuracy of ESN predictions provide an efficient framework for real-time forecasting in dynamically evolving systems.

entry.title: Partial Multistep Prediction of Chaotic Time Series: What Remains Predictable beyond the Horizon of Predictability?
entry.summary: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions limits long-horizon prediction of chaotic systems even for deterministic dynamics, yet some dynamical information may remain recoverable after precise state information is lost. Recursive multistep methods are fragile because they reuse each intermediate prediction as input, allowing local errors to propagate through the rollout. We investigate whether partial multistep prediction can recover predictive information beyond the predictability horizon by omitting intermediate positions instead of assigning them unreliable values. The method uses a lightweight pattern-based local predictor. We analyze partial trajectories generated by different omission patterns and quantify the trade-off between accuracy on retained positions and the fraction classified as non-predictable. Experiments on the Lorenz system show that admissible masks contain trajectories that remain accurate far beyond the horizon of predictability, and an agreement-based ensemble recovers part of this information without future observations at the cost of a growing rejected fraction. At short horizons a broad accepted subset retains accuracy at moderate rejection, whereas at long horizons positive geometric skill requires increasingly strong selection. In this regime retained predictions no longer localize the state within a Lorenz scroll but still identify the occupied scroll, so topological structure outlasts geometric accuracy. A noise-based control reproduces this survival only after tuning of its perturbation scale, unlike masking. Across a heterogeneous collection of chaotic systems the ensemble strictly extends the positive-$R^2$ horizon of the recursive baseline for every retained system.

entry.title: Stability of inverse cascade in NLS Wave turbulence
entry.summary: We study the stability of the inverse cascade in the 3D Nonlinear Schrodinger Wave Kinetic Equation (WKE) in the presence and absence of a condensate. Using theoretical arguments supported by numerical simulation, we show that, the Kolmogorov-Zakharov solution is stable with respect to small isotropic perturbations in the absence of a condensate. Conversely, introducing a condensate component leads to a growth of the condensate occupation and ultimately destabilizes the inverse cascade. The system then evolves towards a new steady-state whose properties depend on the condensate dissipation rate.

entry.title: Nonadiabatic dynamics under slow parametric modulation in nonlinear graphene resonators
entry.summary: Resonantly driven nonlinear systems, from superconducting circuits to nanomechanical resonators, are often described in a rotating frame, where amplitude and phase evolve slowly within a fixed landscape of stable and unstable states. How such systems behave when this landscape moves on their intrinsic timescale remains to be understood. Here, we exploit the strong tension sensitivity of a graphene drum's resonance frequency to reshape the rotating-frame phase space of a bistable mechanical mode in real time, combining an MHz-frequency resonant drive with kHz-frequency tension modulation. When the modulation rate becomes comparable to the mechanical relaxation rate, adiabatic tracking of the fixed points breaks down. Instead, parametric instabilities emerge in the slow dynamics at frequencies set by libration around these points rather than by the mechanical resonance; stronger modulation drives period doubling and chaos. A slow-variable theory predicts where the instabilities occur, and Melnikov analysis captures the onset of chaos. These results show that the rotating frame itself can be parametrically driven, offering a general route to controlling nonadiabatic dynamics in systems ranging from Josephson bifurcation amplifiers to cold atoms.

entry.title: Seven Limit Cycles in a Periodically Forced Three-Zone Equation
entry.summary: We construct a seven-cycle example for a periodically forced scalar equation with a continuous three-zone piecewise-linear nonlinearity. Symbolic integration and linear elimination reduce the four-flight matching conditions to two equations in the residence times. The competing exterior visits produce an additional turn of the critical response and lead to the rational parameters $(A,B,μ)=(9,3/2,181363/100000)$. At these parameters, finite Taylor estimates give three sign changes of the return displacement. Scalar order, analyticity along transverse itineraries, and half-period reflection then establish at least seven distinct isolated periodic orbits on the phase cylinder.

entry.title: Kinetic Equations and Turbulence in Large $N$ Vector and SYK-like Models
entry.summary: We apply large $N$ expansion techniques to derive kinetic equations for strongly coupled, far-from-equilibrium field theories with $O(N)$ symmetry. For large $N$ vector models, the quasi-classical approximation holds. Incorporating arbitrary momentum-dependent interactions, we show the dynamics obey the standard kinetic equation, with the scattering amplitude given by the retarded propagator of the auxiliary Hubbard-Stratonovich field. This has broad applications to systems like spin wave and Langmuir ion-acoustic turbulence. For large $N$ random coupling (SYK-like) models in $d$ dimensions, leading-order melon diagrams induce order-one propagator renormalization and finite spectral width. The corresponding kinetic equation, unlike those for standard weakly interacting systems, does not have a local-in-time collision integral. We find evidence for a stationary, scale-invariant infrared solution, revealing a potentially novel strong turbulence scaling exponent.

entry.title: Beyond RMSE and Granger Gain: Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Entropy for Nonlinear Predictive Coupling
entry.summary: We investigate whether the past of an auxiliary time series provides predictive information about a target beyond that contained in the target's own history. We compare matched out-of-sample target-only and target-plus-source forecasts and introduce the forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE) predictive-causality framework, where predictive causality is understood in the Granger sense: auxiliary history is informative when it improves prediction beyond the target's own past. FEDE quantifies how the full signed forecast-error distribution changes across prediction horizons. Controlled nonlinear benchmarks hide source-target dependence behind nonlinear transformations not supplied to the predictors. LightGBM recovers these hidden channels, whereas Ridge does not. Across four equal-power nonlinearities and four noise levels, the mean response-sensitivity statistic for FEDE remains 29.00, 27.47, 23.22, and 28.67, compared with 14.09, 10.68, 12.67, and 12.71 for mean log-RMSE gain. Directional and source controls separate the true source-to-target channel from the reverse direction and from independent periodic, quasiperiodic, chaotic, and autoregressive auxiliaries. Chronological Granger-style comparisons show strong model-form dependence: a degree-2 polynomial model is exceptionally sensitive to the matched quadratic channel but becomes weak or oppositely aligned for other nonlinearities, while basic convergent cross mapping is weak or directionally inconsistent in this stochastic, partly non-invertible setting. FEDE remains positively aligned across all 108 tested combinations of window length, history length, and maximum forecast horizon. Together, these results establish FEDE as a sensitive and robust horizon-resolved tool that extracts predictive information beyond conventional error-magnitude measures when the nonlinear interaction form is unknown. Code available in Zenodo.

entry.title: Information transfer as a new indicator of approaching local bifurcations: saddle-node, pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations
entry.summary: Early warning signals are key tools for anticipating qualitative changes in the dynamics of complex systems. In this work, we investigate whether an information-theoretic measure designed to characterize directional causal dependencies between observables can provide early warning of the approach to bifurcations. The measure considered is the rate of information transfer, which has been successfully applied to characterize directional dependencies in a broad range of fields, from economics to climate science. Three fundamental local bifurcations are considered: saddle-node, pitchfork, and Hopf bifurcations. We first investigate idealized (quasi-)potential stochastic systems for which analytical expressions for the rate of information transfer can be derived. Distinct signatures are found for the three bifurcation types. In particular, the rate of information transfer displays a strong increase and divergence when approaching the saddle-node bifurcation, whereas smoother but systematic changes are found near the pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations. The approach is then tested using low-order climate models exhibiting the same types of bifurcations. The results confirm that changes in the rate of information transfer can precede the corresponding dynamical transitions, suggesting that directional information transfer provides a useful complementary early-warning indicator for detecting the approach to critical transitions in nonlinear stochastic systems.

entry.title: Cyclotomic Structure and Exact Recurrences in Floquet Many-Body Quantum Dynamics
entry.summary: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit a wide range of complex dynamics, including chaos. Yet, at special parameter values, their evolution can recur exactly. Several quantum protocols have recently been proposed that exploit exact Floquet recurrences to demonstrate genuine quantum advantage. Such recurrences can be studied through the arithmetic structure of the Floquet unitary. In this work, we establish a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact recurrence and determine the minimal recurrence period when one exists. Because recurrence is a global property of the unitary, it holds for every initial state. Applying our framework requires only knowledge of the number field associated with the Hamiltonian parameters. We demonstrate the method using the kicked Ising chain, establishing exact recurrences in both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes. We further show that, in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic--a resource for quantum computation--is generated at intermediate times and undergoes exact periodic revivals enforced by the recurrence of the full Floquet unitary. By connecting number theory, quantum many-body dynamics, and quantum information, our work shows that exact recurrence extends beyond Clifford circuits and opens new avenues for magic generation and quantum hardware benchmarking.

entry.title: Bifurcation Structure of Double Hysteresis and Isolated Branches in a Parametric Duffing Nanoresonator
entry.summary: Direct and parametric driving together generate nonlinear response structures beyond conventional Duffing hysteresis, including multiple switching regions and isolated branches. Understanding how these structures are connected requires identifying the bifurcations that reorganize the response as the parametric excitation is varied. At a phase difference of 45 degrees between the direct and parametric excitations, we experimentally and analytically determine how the steady-state response changes as the parametric excitation is increased. A single resonance peak first splits into two while the response remains single valued. Two successive cusp bifurcations then create two saddle-node pairs and establish a double-hysteretic response. At the parametric-instability threshold, one saddle node of each pair is displaced towards unbounded amplitude and detuning, and an isolated-branch structure emerges above threshold. A parametric representation of the steady state distinguishes amplitude extrema from genuine saddle-node bifurcations and provides analytical conditions for these changes. Measurements on a dielectrically actuated pre-stressed SiN nanostring reproduce the predicted response and associated switching behavior. These results establish the bifurcation pathway connecting the different response structures at this phase configuration, providing a systematic basis for controlling multistability and switching in parametrically driven nonlinear resonators.

entry.title: Limit cycles govern wave energy accumulation in space-time-varying materials
entry.summary: We study the amplification and concentration of wave energy in smooth, periodic space-time media through the dynamics of the characteristic curves of the associated wave equation. In an impedance-matched setting, we show that stable limit cycles attract neighbouring characteristics, focusing the wave energy density. The exponential attraction rate is estimated analytically from the system's Lyapunov exponent. We further show that the attraction of characteristics and energy accumulation persist under a range of nonperiodic perturbations. Finally, we present a Floquet-Fourier numerical method for computing stable and unstable limit cycles and their attraction rates. Throughout, we exemplify the results using the example of modulation given by a superposition of travelling waves, revealing saddle--node bifurcations where limit cycles may appear depending on the relative wave speeds. Full-wave simulations confirm that the characteristic mechanism continues to describe energy accumulation beyond the impedance-matched case.

entry.title: Reverse quantum aging: Restoring rhythmicity from quantum aging state
entry.summary: Quantum aging transition has recently been reported, whereby the oscillatory dynamics of a network of globally coupled quantum self-sustained oscillators is degraded sharply when the fraction of inactive nodes exceeds a critical value. Here we explore the reverse process: the revival of rhythmic dynamics from an aged state in a quantum oscillator network by introducing a controlled incoherent single-boson pumping channel. Using a self-consistent quantum master equation in the Lindblad form for globally coupled active--inactive quantum Stuart--Landau oscillators, we show that increasing the pumping strength progressively suppresses the aging transition and eventually eliminates it, restoring rhythmicity even when all oscillators are inactive. Remarkably, complete compensation of the coupling-induced dissipative loss is not required; a substantially weaker pumping strength is sufficient to eliminate the aging transition. We show that the revival is governed by a redistribution of the Fock-state population of the inactive oscillators toward higher-occupation states. Our results establish controlled incoherent pumping as an effective mechanism for restoring dynamical robustness in quantum oscillator networks.

entry.title: Geometric Transition of Latent Dynamics in Intermittent Chaos: SVD-based Effective Dimension for Detection and Proactive Control
entry.summary: This paper investigates the geometric detection of latent dynamic transitions (where the latent space is defined as a finite-dimensional state space reconstructed via a delay-embedding Hankel matrix) in mutually coupled phase-locked loops (PLLs) exhibiting on-off intermittent chaos. We propose a data-driven approach to identify the transition of the effective dimension in latent dynamics as a precursor to physical bursting events. By applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to a Hankel matrix constructed from high-resolution oversampled data, we extract the effective dimension that reflects the dynamical shift of intrinsic variables - from a synchronized two-dimensional manifold to a higher-dimensional chaotic state - prior to the actual burst. This geometric indicator enables a proactive, event-driven intervention using Pyragas-type delayed feedback control, which is activated only when the detected dimension exceeds a critical threshold. Simulation results demonstrate that this geometric precursor effectively compensates for control latencies and substantially reduces accumulated control energy compared to conventional continuous feedback. The findings establish a methodological strategy for stabilizing infinite-dimensional delayed systems by exploiting early warning signals embedded in dimensional transitions of latent dynamics.

entry.title: Multivariate phase-space interpretation of ensemble forecasts: A comparison of physical and AI models
entry.summary: Ensemble forecasts from the ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) and the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-ENS) are compared using a multi-dimensional evaluation framework. Within this framework, the uncertainty is interpreted as the linear subspace spanned by the ensemble members in phase space, from which various geometric properties are extracted. As revealed by the analysis, the error does not entirely lie in this subspace, but is reasonably well calibrated in all directions. Moreover, the framework allows to quantify that this subspace critically depends on the number of ensemble members, suggesting that the current setups only partially represent the uncertainty subspace. This phase-space interpretation furthermore allows a direct comparison of the error-representation patterns of AIFS-ENS and IFS by computing the principal angles between the subspaces: IFS and AIFS ensemble subspaces do not entirely overlap in phase space, even though they were shown to have similar abilities to represent the amplitude and the structure of the error.

entry.title: Universal Boolean Computation in Negatively Coupled Circle Map Lattices
entry.summary: We investigate the computational capabilities of a one-dimensional lattice of negatively coupled circle maps in its traveling wave regime. We interpret propagating waves as information carriers and exploit their interactions to implement Boolean logic. The logical states are encoded by the propagation direction of the traveling waves, while the presence or absence of a wave at a designated output location represents the logical output. Using controlled wave collisions, we demonstrate the realization of NAND and NOR gates along with other basic gates. Since NAND and NOR operations are functionally complete, the results establish that the traveling wave regime of the negatively coupled circle-map lattice supports universal Boolean computation in principle. The demonstrated logical operations remain valid over a finite range of the coupling strength εand map parameter ω, indicating robustness of the computational scheme to parameter variations. Our results therefore demonstrate that computational functionality can emerge from the collective nonlinear dynamics of a coupled map lattice, providing a con- nection between the dynamical properties of traveling wave states and collision based information processing.

entry.title: Random wave chaos on momentum-fractionated microstate geometries
entry.summary: We study the role of momentum fractionation in the development of chaos on smooth 3-charge supergravity solutions of D1-D5 theory, specifically momentum-fractionated superstrata. We probe the chaos through the dynamics of null geodesics and waves. On fractionated backgrounds, both geodesics and waves show uniformly strong chaos (large chaotic sea and near-perfect agreement with the Berry random wave hypothesis). In contrast, geodesics and waves on single-mode (non-fractionated) superstrata are closer to separability (although still chaotic). We discuss a possibility that such dichotomy can be related to the expectation that monotone BPS states are less chaotic than fortuitous ones. Finally, we explain why our chaos probes are meaningful for microstate geometries even though they become trivial in the black hole limit.

entry.title: Inferred and Residual Parameter Interactions in Syntax Dynamics
entry.summary: What makes natural languages diversify, in their syntactic structure, even when sharing a largely common origin? We refine our simple model, which focuses on the glassy dynamics induced by a network of interactions between syntactic parameters. Distinguishing between symmetric interaction weights that can be inferred from the observed statistics of syntax across many languages, and additional asymmetric weights assigned at random, we show that both components are needed, with similar overall strength, to account for plausible long-term syntactic dynamics. An approximate balance can combine the glassy metastability provided by the inferred weights with the chaotic diversification induced by the residual asymmetric weights.

entry.title: Energy Transmission and Harmonic Propagation in Unidirectionally Coupled Plasma Oscillator Networks
entry.summary: We investigate signal transmission in a network of unidirectionally coupled plasma oscillators, where only the first oscillator is driven by a weak periodic input. As the signal propagates through the network, nonlinear interactions generate higher-order harmonic components. Spectral analysis identifies five distinct transmission patterns for the fundamental frequency and odd harmonics, and four patterns for even harmonics, encompassing damped propagation, undamped transmission, and localized amplification. The transmission characteristics are governed by both the coupling strength and system parameters. Furthermore, we analyze how variations in these key parameters shape the overall signal dynamics.

entry.title: Nonlinear Signal Transmission and Harmonic Generation in Plasma Oscillator Chain with Coupling Asymmetry
entry.summary: We investigate signal transmission in a one-dimensional chain of $n$ locally coupled plasma oscillators with asymmetric bidirectional coupling $(ε_1,ε_2)$. Our results reveal a clear contrast between symmetric and asymmetric interactions: while symmetric coupling suppresses signal propagation, coupling asymmetry enables efficient nonlinear transmission across the network. In particular, sustained long range transmission is achieved when the forward coupling strength exceeds the backward coupling strength ($ε_1 > ε_2$), as demonstrated through a comprehensive phase diagram in the $(ε_1,ε_2)$ parameter space. Furthermore, under asymmetric diffusive coupling, signal transmission can persist even when the first few oscillators in the chain undergo oscillation death. A central finding of this study is the intrinsic generation of higher harmonics induced by nonlinear interactions, leading to a pronounced reversal of vibrational resonance. This nonlinear redistribution of energy facilitates selective amplification and robust propagation of specific frequency components.

entry.title: Wake-induced dynamics of soft-impact oscillators: Analysis and electronic experimental validation
entry.summary: This article presents an electronic experimental validation of discontinuity-induced bifurcations, including period-adding cascades, in a wake-induced dynamical system subjected to soft impacts. A cylindrical structure immersed in a cross-flow undergoes vortex-induced vibrations and interacts with a movable barrier during the upper and lower branches of the response. The structural motion is modelled as a harmonic oscillator, while the fluctuating lift is represented by a Van der Pol oscillator. The soft contact interaction between the structure and the movable barrier is modelled using a bilinear restoring force, resulting in a piecewise-smooth wake-oscillator system. A systematic numerical investigation reveals period-adding cascades of periodic orbits interspersed with chaotic responses as the barrier distance and fluid-flow velocity are varied. The results are experimentally validated using an inductorless electronic analogue of the piecewise-smooth wake model constructed from operational amplifiers and implemented on a printed-circuit board to improve experimental robustness. The route to instability of the periodic and aperiodic responses is further characterized using Floquet multipliers and Lyapunov exponents. A zero-time transverse discontinuity mapping is implemented to account for the evolution of perturbations in the local neighborhood of the discontinuity boundary during stability analysis. The combined numerical, experimental, and stability analyses demonstrate the role of soft impacts in generating complex nonlinear responses in the wake-induced system.

entry.title: Quantum extreme learning for forecasting experimental chaotic electronic circuits
entry.summary: Quantum reservoir computing and its special case, quantum extreme learning, are powerful tools for predicting classical discrete time-series with quantum devices. Forecasting continuous signals, however, requires careful discretization as oversampling artificially boosts short-term accuracy but fails over realistic intervals, while undersampling captures too few features and yields poor predictions. Here, we experimentally generate four continuous time-series signals from a chaotic electronic circuit for forecasting with quantum extreme learning. Since simplified circuit models do not fully capture real behaviour, it is unclear whether algorithms that predict simulated time-series also work for experimental signals. We address discretization via two approaches: (i) sampling local peaks/troughs; and (ii) uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale. The former captures resonant behaviour, while the latter fully captures chaotic features as well as allowing the reconstruction of chaotic attractors. Our algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental signals, demonstrating its power for continuous signal processing on near-term quantum simulators, and remains robust against moderate decoherence.

entry.title: Silent breakdown of the perturbative polarization expansion in the terahertz regime
entry.summary: Nonlinear optics expands the polarization in powers of the drive and retains only the lowest-order terms. This truncation is safe at optical frequencies, where the convergence field lies far above the damage threshold. In the terahertz regime, phonon polaritons enhance the nonlinear susceptibilities by orders of magnitude, lowering the convergence field into the sub-damage range and opening a window in which the expansion fails while the crystal remains recoverable. We term this window silent breakdown. At resonance, the nearest singularities of the driven lattice mode are a complex-conjugate pair of branch points below the multistability threshold, so the response remains smooth and single-valued even though the $χ^{\left( n \right)}$ description fails. The convergence field scales as $Q^{-3/2}$, so sharpening a resonance enhances the nonlinearity but narrows the range over which the expansion applies. It follows from the mode shift $S$ alone, $E_{\mathrm{conv}}=E_{\mathrm{ref}}(3\sqrt{3}QS)^{-1/2}$, giving 2$\sim$9 MV/cm for $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{3}$. Since resonant enhancement is central to terahertz nonlinear optics, this boundary defines the field range over which susceptibility-based descriptions are quantitatively reliable.

entry.title: Understanding Latent-Dimension Scaling in Dynamical-System Learning through Spectral Reliability
entry.summary: In deep learning, approximation theory motivates increasing representation size. We ask whether this benefit extends to dynamics learning through autoregressive prediction. We analyze the learned time evolution through the eigenstructure of Koopman operators, using relative residuals to detect spurious eigenpairs arising even as one-step error falls. For bounded Koopman operators, we show that minimal residuals over learned dictionary spaces converge pointwise to their full-space counterparts as these spaces approximate the observable space in $L^2$. Our hypothesis is that Koopman spectral reliability helps explain how consistently rollout error decreases with increasing dimension. We compare two models of a shared Koopman autoencoder trained alternately for reconstruction and latent evolution, using latent-prediction loss (one-step prediction errors in latent coordinates) or spectral-residual loss (relative residuals of candidate eigenpairs). Across six chaotic systems, both models reduced median windowed rollout error from smallest to largest dimension. The spectral-residual model achieved lower medians than the latent-prediction model for all systems and dimensions, and its median fell by a larger factor in every system. Its median decreased monotonically with dimension in four systems, against one for latent prediction. Against four baseline families, its mean valid prediction times were nearly always longer. At the largest dimension under two-stage training, we compared eigenvalue positions with each learned dictionary's residual contours. Spectral-residual eigenvalues concentrated in low-residual regions, whereas latent-prediction eigenvalues also appeared in high-residual regions, consistent with the hypothesis.

entry.title: Energy-barrier characterization of secured basins in coupled oscillators with inertia
entry.summary: The second-order Kuramoto model captures rotor dynamics relevant to synchronization in power grids. In actual power grids, violation of angle-stability limits can trigger protective actions that are not included in the model, restricting its validity to trajectories that remain within these limits. We therefore define the secured basin as the region of disturbance space comprising disturbances whose trajectories remain within the angle-stability limits throughout the transient. We then characterize the secured basin through energy barriers, quantifying their characteristic energy scale and heterogeneity across perturbation directions. Across seven power-grid models, this characterization revealed angle-stability vulnerabilities overlooked when stability is assessed solely by the final synchronization state. It also showed that the two energy-barrier measures characterizing the secured basin exhibit distinct associations with structural connectivity and dynamical parameters. This characterization further offers practical advantages, as energy thresholds derived from state-space perturbations remain effective in distinguishing secured and unsecured outcomes under short-duration power disturbances and can be estimated efficiently by concentrating simulations near the secured-basin boundary. Overall, the secured-basin framework provides a useful basis for distinguishing node-level structural and dynamical influences on transient stability in oscillator networks with synchronization constraints.

entry.title: Three-dimensional Lagrangian ecosystems: carbon dynamics and potential for artificial fertilization
entry.summary: Transient supplies of nutrients to the surface ocean, both natural and artificial, stimulate blooms of phytoplankton and the formation of organic matter, driving air-sea gradients and uptake of CO$_2$. However, quantifying the associated carbon budget remains challenging, as it requires tracking the coupled biophysical evolution of water masses while they are transported, stretched and diluted. Here, we present an idealized three-dimensional model that describes biomass production and carbon dynamics within a Lagrangian patch in the ocean. The framework reproduces observed biogeochemical patterns from an artificial fertilization experiment and provides integrated metrics for the local carbon budget. Utilizing large ensembles of simulations, we examine the sensitivity of patch-scale primary production and carbon uptake to biochemical and physical factors. Our results show that patch dilution can enhance the ecosystem response, and how carbon uptake is sensitive to initial injected area, horizontal divergence and vertical diffusivity. In the context of renewed interest in ocean fertilization strategies for climate mitigation, our approach can thus provide quantitative tools to assess their efficacy and potential.

entry.title: A Second-Order Asymptotic Expansion for Nonlinear Filtering in the Lorenz--63 System
entry.summary: A challenge in nonlinear filtering is to incorporate nonlinear effects into approximations of the conditional mean while retaining a finite-dimensional recursive algorithm. We derive a second-order asymptotic expansion of the filtering mean with respect to the system-noise intensity. We apply this expansion to the Lorenz--63 model, a prototypical three-dimensional chaotic dynamical system. The first-order approximation is computed using a Kalman--Bucy filter for the system linearized around the deterministic reference trajectory. The second-order correction incorporates the Hessian of the Lorenz--63 drift and is computed through a closed recursive system with 3+9+18=30 independent scalar components. The full system, including the reference trajectory and the first-order mean and covariance, has 42 independent scalar components. To support stable tracking of chaotic trajectories over long time intervals, we introduce recentering of the expansion and redistribution of Gaussian components between expansion orders. In the numerical experiments, we compare the proposed algorithm with an ensemble transform Kalman filter (ETKF) as a practical benchmark and a particle filter (PF) as a numerical reference. Under the full-observation settings, the proposed algorithm achieves a lower root-mean-square error relative to the truth and a smaller distance to the 10,000-particle PF reference than the 20-member ETKF. These results suggest that the proposed second-order extension of Kalman filtering has the potential to balance filtering accuracy and computational cost.

entry.title: Heterogeneity-induced chaos in globally coupled Stuart--Landau oscillators
entry.summary: We show that linear-growth-rate heterogeneity combined with complex global coupling can generate quasiperiodicity and chaos in a finite population of Stuart-Landau oscillators with identical natural frequencies and no Kerr-type nonlinear frequency shift. Lyapunov spectra identify limit cycles, quasiperiodic tori, and chaotic attractors, while the order-parameter amplitude exhibits signatures consistent with period-doubling-like transitions towards chaos. We further derive a finite-size invariant manifold of vanishing-order-parameter phase-locked solutions represented by closed polygons with fixed side lengths and demonstrate their configuration-dependent transverse stability. Ensemble sampling reveals pronounced coexistence among polygonal and ordinary phase-locked cycles, quasiperiodic tori, and chaotic attractors. An amplitude-time rescaling identifies the leading parameter approximately organizing the regime boundaries and the similar bifurcation and multistability patterns. These results advance our understanding of collective dynamics in amplitude-inclusive oscillator networks by revealing how heterogeneity and complex coupling jointly shape dynamical complexity, bifurcation structure, and multistability.

entry.title: Gravitational-wave signatures of spinning particles around rotating hairy black holes
entry.summary: We study how the spin of a compact secondary and a gravitational-decoupling deformation of the Kerr geometry are imprinted on gravitational waves from strong-field eccentric motion around a rotating black hole. The orbit is evolved with the Mathisson--Papapetrou--Dixon equations under the Tulczyjew spin supplementary condition, and the radiation is computed with the numerical-kludge method. The deformation describes a black hole only below a critical curve in the plane of the two hair parameters. The spin of the secondary pulls the pericenter inward and, above a critical value, carries the particle into the black hole. The hair raises this capture threshold, from $S\simeq0.66$ in Kerr to $0.9$ and above close to the horizon boundary, because it reduces the effective mass near the black hole. The emitted signal remains a discrete comb of orbital harmonics: the spin strengthens the pericenter bursts and shifts power toward higher harmonics, while both the spin and the hair leave their main imprint through an accumulated dephasing. The imprint of the hair is controlled by the parameter that sets the radial reach of the deformation, disappears in the Kerr-like limit of the family, and is amplified by the spin of the secondary. For a source at $2$ Gpc with $M=10^6M_\odot$ and $μ=10M_\odot$, a $6.8$ h segment of the signal carries a signal-to-noise ratio of about $1.4$ in LISA, $2.7$ in Taiji and $0.9$ in TianQin. Within the same segment the more extended deformations become distinguishable from Kerr, first in Taiji; since this holds for a nonspinning secondary, it applies directly to astrophysical EMRIs. The spin-induced frequency shifts are linear in the spin, so the large spins used here are a magnified illustration of a dephasing that, for realistic secondaries, accumulates to a phase of order a radian over an inspiral.

entry.title: The interface of data assimilation and machine learning
entry.summary: Data assimilation (DA) is the process of combining forecasts from a model with observations in order to optimally estimate the state of a system. This is critical for chaotic systems, such as the atmosphere, since if observations are not continually assimilated the model will quickly lose skill. DA is routinely performed (usually every 6 hours) at operational forecasting centres around the world. In this article we discuss the interface of machine learning (ML) and DA. This is still an emerging and quickly developing field, and this article tries to give an overview of some of the main topics and methods.

entry.title: Number Theory of Decaying Turbulence 3: Comparing with Physical and Numerical Experiments
entry.summary: We compare the predictions of the Euler-ensemble solution of freely decaying incompressible turbulence with simulations and experiments: the scaling function of the energy spectrum, the index of the second-order structure function and the decay laws. The predictions have a fixed shape; only their normalization and scale are fitted. In the final $4096^3$ direct numerical simulations of Rodhiya and Sreenivasan, the turbulent attractor is selected by a parabola law for the growth of the bulk length. Along it the collapsed spectrum depends only on the instantaneous Reynolds number, identically for Saffman and Loitsyansky initial spectra; extrapolated to infinite Reynolds number, it agrees with the theory to 1% in the bulk of the enstrophy range, below the dissipation range. The energy balance holds exactly. The energy integral of the theory diverges in the infrared, so energy and enstrophy depend on how a finite flow cuts off the spectrum: with a sharp cutoff $k_0$, the decay laws, energy $\propto t^{-5/4}$ and enstrophy $\propto t^{-9/4}$, are reached only when the cutoff enters the $k^{-7/2}$ tail of the spectrum. Such a cutoff is only an estimate; the reliable test is the bulk of the spectrum. Fitted to the simulations, the cutoff lies at the lower edge of the bulk, where the spectrum still carries the initial data, and the decay exponents depend on the initial infrared spectrum. In the Max Planck wind tunnel at $Re_λ$ up to 5779, the longitudinal index extrapolated to infinite Reynolds number matches the odd ensemble with one scale parameter at large separations, where standard crossover forms fail. The freely decaying turbulent blob of Matsuzawa et al. is too small, too inhomogeneous and too weak to display the attractor. The theory is derived in the first two papers of this series.

entry.title: Classical chaotic signatures in Krylov space
entry.summary: In recent years, Krylov space approaches have emerged as a useful framework for characterizing dynamical chaos in a wide variety of physical systems. However, the connection between Krylov dynamics and the established structures of classical chaos remains largely unexplored. Classical chaos is characterized by exponential stretching and mixing. For quantum maps with a classical limit, we show that these two signatures are encoded in different structures within Krylov space: stretching is encoded in the geometry of the Krylov operators as determined by the Lyapunov exponent, while mixing manifests itself as an exponential decay of the Arnoldi sequences in agreement with the Ruelle-Pollicott resonances.
